opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is that I've become somewhat more optimistic that we can get a lot of safety out of approaches that don't require us to solve alignment in the deep sense, but also more pessimistic about how much effort will actually go into those approaches.

A few years ago I mostly thought about this as: either you figure out how to make the AI actually want what you want, or you're in a lot of trouble. Since then, a lot of my work at Redwood has been on AI control. The question there is: suppose the models you're deploying are actively trying to undermine you. Can you still set things up so they can't cause a catastrophe, and so you still get useful work out of them? You might do that by monitoring them with trusted weaker models, auditing suspicious actions, restricting permissions, and so on.

When I first started thinking about that, I expected it to fall apart pretty quickly. In practice, it seems like there's a substantial regime where it works decently well. That's the regime where models are roughly as capable as, or somewhat more capable than, the people they're replacing, but not wildly superhuman. And that's exactly the regime you care about for "AIs that can obsolete AGI researchers." Those are the systems you'd want to use to help solve the harder problems later. So technically I think the problem is more tractable than I used to.

What's made me more pessimistic is the sociological side. I used to imagine a world where AI developers took these risks fairly seriously, moved somewhat cautiously, and spent a meaningful fraction of their resources on safety. Now I think the more realistic picture is that companies are racing, timelines are short, and safety teams will have small budgets and limited political capital inside their organizations. So a lot of my thinking has shifted toward the question: what can a pretty small team of people do, at a company that doesn't care very much, to reduce risk as much as possible? I call that sort of the "rushed, unreasonable developer" scenario, and I think it's more likely than the scenario where everyone's being careful.

Put those together and my bottom line is something like this. The problem is more solvable than I feared if people actually try. But I'm less confident people will try, so a lot of the value is in making the cheap interventions really cheap and really well-understood, so that even a careless developer adopts them.

r001.rationale: He describes AI control measures such as monitoring, auditing, and restricting permissions, and says they work decently well in the capability regime relevant to systems that could obsolete AGI researchers, making the problem more tractable.

r002.rationale: He says he is more pessimistic about how much effort companies will put into these approaches, citing racing, short timelines, small safety budgets, and limited political capital.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my view has shifted in a direction that's maybe a little surprising given what I work on. A few years ago, I would have said that the core problem is basically unsolved in a deep technical sense, and that you'd need major conceptual breakthroughs to have any real confidence that models that are as capable as our best researchers aren't scheming against you. And I still think we don't have those breakthroughs. But I've come to think the practical problem is more tractable than I expected, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that the models we're actually getting look a lot more like something you can study and iterate on than the picture I had in my head. They're trained on human data, they reason in something that looks like natural language, they're not wildly superhuman along every axis at once. That means a lot of the techniques that seemed hopeless in the abstract, like reading the model's reasoning, running it in situations where it thinks it has an opportunity to misbehave, having other copies of the model check its work, actually have real purchase. None of it is airtight, but it's a lot better than nothing.

The second is the control framing, which is the thing I've spent most of my time on. The idea is that instead of trying to guarantee the model is aligned, you ask: suppose it's not, suppose it's actively trying to undermine you. Can you still deploy it in a way where it can't cause a catastrophe? And when you actually sit down and think about what a model at roughly human-researcher level could do if it wanted to sabotage you, it's genuinely constrained. It doesn't have unlimited affordances. It has to act through tools you can log, it's doing work you can audit at least some of the time, and it has to coordinate with other instances that may well rat it out. So you get a bunch of leverage from pretty mundane security and monitoring measures, the kind of thing you'd do for an untrusted contractor.

So the way I'd summarize it is: I've become more optimistic that we can get through the period where AIs are roughly as capable as our researchers without a disaster, even if alignment is unsolved. The place where I've become more pessimistic, or at least not more optimistic, is what happens after that. Control-style measures get much weaker once the models are substantially smarter than the people checking them. So the bet is really that you use that window to have the AIs do the alignment research we failed to do ourselves. And that's a somewhat uncomfortable bet, because you're relying on systems you don't fully trust to help you build systems you can trust more. But I think it's a much better position than I would have predicted we'd be in.

The other big update, honestly, is less technical and more about institutions. Even if the techniques work, the question of whether labs will actually implement them under competitive pressure, with real costs to speed, is a lot of where the risk lives. I used to think of that as somebody else's problem. I don't anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says practical measures may help get through the period when AIs are roughly as capable as researchers, but says control measures weaken once models are substantially smarter. It does not claim those measures would substantially reduce risk from AIs capable of obsoleting AGI researchers.

r002.rationale: The response identifies lab implementation under competitive pressure as a major risk and says this concern is newly salient to him. It does not state that he has substantially lowered his expectations about how many mitigation measures AI companies will implement.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more optimistic that we can get useful work out of those systems without first solving the whole alignment problem. I’d now put more weight on approaches where we assume the model might be trying to undermine us, and ask whether we can nevertheless check its work, limit what it can do, and catch attempts to cause trouble.

That seems particularly relevant for systems that can automate AGI research. Being capable enough to replace a researcher doesn’t automatically mean being capable enough to defeat every safeguard we can put around it. There might be a window where these systems are enormously useful, including for safety research, but still possible to control.

The big uncertainty is how large that window is. If we move very quickly from systems that can replace researchers to systems that can easily outthink our whole oversight process, this buys us much less. So I’m more optimistic about handling that initial level of capability than about the claim that everything after it will be fine.

r001.rationale: The response expresses greater optimism about checking, limiting, and monitoring capable systems, but it does not say these known, individually manageable measures would probably substantially reduce misalignment risk.

r002.rationale: The response says nothing about Buck’s expectations for how many mitigation measures AI companies will implement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more optimistic about our ability to use those AIs to help with alignment research, but I’m still pretty worried about whether we can safely get to that point.

There’s a tempting argument that, once you have AIs that are better than humans at doing alignment research, you can just ask them to solve the problem. And that really is a potentially enormous advantage. But you have to be able to trust the process by which you’re getting that research. If the models are trying to undermine your safety work, then having them produce very sophisticated arguments that you can’t independently evaluate is a pretty dangerous situation.

So I’d separate two questions: how hard is the remaining alignment research, and how hard is it to safely get useful work out of the systems doing it? Automation could make the first question much less daunting without resolving the second.

That’s part of why I’m interested in control: can we arrange things so that, even if these models are trying to cause problems, we can catch them or prevent them from succeeding? You don’t necessarily need complete confidence in their motivations to get useful work from them. But you do need a convincing story about why your safeguards work, and that gets harder as the models become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using AI for alignment research and control safeguards, but does not state that a known set of individually manageable measures would probably substantially reduce misalignment risk.

r002.rationale: The response says nothing about Buck Shlegeris lowering his expectations for how many mitigation measures AI companies will implement.
